This room needs WebGL 2 to draw, and this browser has not got it. The books can still be read: use Catalogue below.

The hidden library

Behind the shelf. Each book is one system that CRR’s grammar was checked against, with how it came out.

Drag to look. Click the floor to walk. Pull a book from the lit shelves.

The ledger

These are retrodictions: checks against things that were already known. The museum’s own scripts ran them, and nobody outside has checked the scripts. They are not proof of anything. A book that fails, or that only restates the textbook, is listed as plainly as one that fits.

Came out asHow manyWhich

Catalogue

Every book in the library, by shelf. The colour of a spine is its verdict, and the verdict is written beside it.

Papers from the cellar

Behind the fire

The back of the hearth is a door. A passage runs behind the chimney, cold after the fire, with a doorway for each room that was too big for a book.

The books hold what was found. These are places to stand inside an idea for a while. Each one says what it models and what it leaves out, and each brings you back here.

The colloquy

Position papers written in the museum, each looking at CRR through one lens. They argue with it and with each other. None of them is evidence that CRR is right, and where a paper proposes a variant of its own it says so.

About this room

A library that the museum keeps out of sight, for one question: when CRR’s grammar is laid over a real system, does it say anything that could have been wrong?

What CRR is

Coherence, Rupture, Regeneration is the museum owner’s own framework. It reads a system as a path round a loop, counts the change, cuts at each half turn, and carries a seed forward. Very little of it is new mathematics. The first book on the mathematics shelf explains it. It is not established science, and nothing in this room shows that it is.

How a book gets here

Each book has a script that writes its prediction down before it looks at the data, runs against real or simulated data, and compares the result with an ordinary baseline from that field. The script writes a results file, and the numbers in the book are copied from that file. A test compares them. Verdicts are one of five words: fits, partly, fails, restates, untestable. Some books are checked against data, some against a theorem or law that already exists, some count or quote a document, and some draw on the owner’s Phoenix record. Each says which.

What this leaves out

These checks look back at things already known, so a fit may be a description found after the fact. The scripts are the museum’s own. Some data is simulated from a field’s standard equations, and each book says so. Counting verdicts is not a measure of truth: the systems were chosen by the people who wrote the books.

Moving about

Drag to look. Click or tap the floor to walk there, or use W A S D or the arrow keys. Click a book on the lit shelves to pull it. In a book, the left and right arrow keys turn to the previous and next book. Escape closes a book, and from the room it takes you back to the museum. The ladder rolls if you push it. Everything can also be reached from the buttons at the bottom, and the Catalogue lists the parts of the house that are not books.
